title: Top of the World
tagline: Two climbers from opposite ends of the Earth reach the same impossible peak together.

scenes.text: Nepal, May 1953. For Tenzing Norgay, this is the seventh attempt on Everest. He has spent more time on this mountain than almost any living person — he knows its ice, its sudden storms, its moods. He calls it Chomolungma: the goddess mother of the world.

scenes.speaker: Tenzing Norgay
scenes.text: I have been to this mountain before. Six times I have tried. Six times the mountain sent me back. This time — this time I believe she will allow it. I do not know why. I only know I feel it.

challenge.instruction: Tenzing's seventh attempt begins with a long march. Lead the porters from Kathmandu to Thyangboche to acclimatise, then up through the Icefall to the South Col and the top.
challenge.fact: Hillary and Tenzing summited at 11:30 AM on 29 May 1953, spending only 15 minutes on top before descending — long enough for photographs and to bury a small cross and some sweets as offerings. The news reached London in time to appear on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

scenes.text: Edmund Hillary is a New Zealand beekeeper who learned mountaineering in the Alps and the Southern Alps of New Zealand. He is not a professional climber — he is simply someone for whom the impossible is interesting. He and Tenzing have been roped together for weeks.

scenes.speaker: Edmund Hillary
scenes.text: The summit ridge is narrow as a knife. Ice on the left, a 10,000-foot drop to Tibet on the right. Tenzing is behind me. Every step burns. I swing the ice-axe and cut a step. Another. Another. Another.

scenes.speaker: Tenzing Norgay
scenes.text: Chomolungma is our mountain — the goddess mother of the world. I am the ninth of thirteen children from a Sherpa family. To stand here is not just my ambition. It is an answer to something the mountain has been asking of my people for a long time.

challenge.instruction: Roped together for weeks, Hillary and Tenzing depend on the lines fixed below them. Link the high camps with exactly the ropes each one needs.
challenge.fact: Hillary always insisted that he and Tenzing summited together as a team, refusing to say who stepped onto the peak first. He later wrote: 'We didn't talk about it much — it didn't seem important.' For the rest of his life, Hillary devoted enormous energy to building schools, hospitals, and water pipelines for the Sherpa communities of Nepal.

scenes.text: They reach the Hillary Step — a 40-foot rock wall at 28,710 feet, just below the summit. No one has climbed it before. On one side: Tibet. On the other: Nepal. Hillary wedges himself into a crack in the ice and chimney-climbs upward.

scenes.speaker: Edmund Hillary
scenes.text: We go for the top at first light. Together. Neither of us could do this alone — and neither of us should have to.

scenes.speaker: Tenzing Norgay
scenes.text: Together. The mountain asks everything of a man. But two men together — perhaps that is something even the mountain must answer.

challenge.instruction: First light, 29 May. Pick a way along the knife-edge ridge and up the Hillary Step to the summit — every step at this height costs twice the breath.
challenge.fact: The 1953 expedition was a meticulous logistical operation: 400 porters, 362 loads of equipment, months of acclimatization. John Hunt's planning was military in precision. But in the end, it came down to two men in the predawn cold, kicking steps into ice above the Hillary Step.

scenes.text: They reached the summit at 11:30 AM on May 29, 1953. Hillary photographed Tenzing holding four flags — Nepal, Britain, the United Nations, and India. Tenzing pressed chocolate and biscuits into the snow as an offering to the Buddhist gods. They spent fifteen minutes on the roof of the world.

scenes.speaker: Edmund Hillary
scenes.text: Well, we knocked the bastard off.

scenes.speaker: Tenzing Norgay
scenes.text: Chomolungma has been kind to us today. I do not feel we have conquered her. She has allowed us to touch her crown — and that is a very different thing.

challenge.instruction: A runner is already on his way down to Namche with The Times's coded message. Decode it — the news must reach London before anyone else hears.
challenge.fact: James Morris of The Times sent the news in a pre-arranged code: 'Snow conditions bad. Advanced base abandoned yesterday. Awaiting improvement' meant that Hillary and Tenzing had reached the top. It reached London on the eve of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation, and the paper broke the story on coronation morning, 2 June 1953.

scenes.text: Back in the world below, the question immediately arose: who stepped on top first? They had agreed, on the mountain, to say nothing. The summit belonged to both of them equally — and that was the only answer they would give.

challenge.instruction: Long before anyone stood on top, surveyors measured the mountain from the plains of India. Chain the triangles from the baseline up to Peak XV.
challenge.fact: The Survey of India first computed the height of Peak XV in 1856 from stations more than 160 km away and named it after Sir George Everest, its former Surveyor General. Tibetans call it Chomolungma, 'Goddess Mother of the World', and Nepalis Sagarmatha, 'Forehead of the Sky'. Its height, 8,848.86 m, was last fixed jointly by Nepal and China in 2020.

scenes.text: Hillary was knighted. Tenzing received the George Medal. Both returned to Nepal and devoted decades to the Himalayan people — Hillary through the Himalayan Trust, which built over 30 schools. Their partnership outlasted the summit.

scenes.speaker: Edmund Hillary
scenes.text: Diego Maradona and Peter Arnett are still in the rival's hand; they will come to the board one by one. Follow them, start the Battlefield where they stand, and fight with Kill mode on. A player with no Great People left is out of the game.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 7 · Conquest. Deploy, move to wherever the rival stands, start the Battlefield there, and attack with Kill mode on until the rival has no Great People left.
challenge.fact: With Kill mode on, a beaten card is discarded instead of returning to hand. A player with no Great People left, in hand or on the board, is out, and the last player standing wins. A kill won in a Great Person's own stat also counts towards their achievement.
